title: Cross-tenant IDOR on all knowledge-base routes (read/write/delete of other organizations' KBs and files)
description: All knowledge-base management routes (`/api/knowledge-bases/*`) perform authentication but no organization-scoping on object lookups. `knowledgeBaseService` queries Prisma by bare record ID, so an authenticated user from any organization can read, modify, and delete another organization's knowledge bases, folders, and uploaded files.
impact: Cross-tenant breach of knowledge-base confidentiality and integrity: an authenticated member of organization A can enumerate knowledge-base IDs and read org B's knowledge bases (names, descriptions, file listings), rename/soft-delete them, and modify or delete org B's uploaded knowledge files. Knowledge bases aggregate a tenant's RAG document corpus, so this exposes another tenant's content metadata and allows destructive modification.
technical_analysis:
Route `src/routes/knowledge-base.routes.ts` guards every endpoint only with `[authenticate, requireModifyAccess]` — a role check, not a tenant check. Handlers call `knowledgeBaseService.findById(request.params.id)` etc. without passing `request.user.orgId`. In `src/services/knowledge-base.service.ts`:
- `findById` (line 69): `prisma.knowledge_bases.findUnique({ where: { id } })` — no `organization_id` filter.
- `update` (line 80) and `delete` (line 91): `update({ where: { id } })` — mutates any org's KB.
- `renameFolder` (200), `deleteFolder` (215), `listFolders` (190): unscoped by organization.
- File handlers in the route operate on `knowledge_files` by bare id.

Contrast with the correctly-scoped pattern in `credential-vault.repository.ts:37` (`findFirst({ where: { id, organization_id } })`), which shows the missing control.
poc_description: 1. Authenticate as a member of org A. 2. GET /api/knowledge-bases/:id with an org B knowledge-base ID — 200 with org B data (organization_id of org B returned). 3. PUT /api/knowledge-bases/:id — renames org B's KB. 4. GET /api/knowledge-bases/:id/files — lists org B file records; PUT .../files/:fileId changes display metadata; DELETE .../files/:fileId removes org B's file record. 5. DELETE /api/knowledge-bases/:id soft-deletes org B's KB.
poc_script_code:
# Reproduce (repo-local, no network):
cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts
# Key assertions from that PoC:
# - GET    /api/knowledge-bases/<ORG_B_KB_ID>          -> 200, data.organization_id == ORG_B
# - PUT    /api/knowledge-bases/<ORG_B_KB_ID>          -> 200, name renamed by org-A user
# - DELETE /api/knowledge-bases/<ORG_B_KB_ID>          -> 204, status='deleted'
# - PUT    /api/knowledge-bases/<ORG_B_KB_ID>/files/<ORG_B_FILE_ID> -> 200, display_name overwritten
# - DELETE /api/knowledge-bases/<ORG_B_KB_ID>/files/<ORG_B_FILE_ID>  -> 204, org-B row removed
remediation_steps: Add organization scoping at the service layer: `findById(id, organizationId)` must use `findFirst({ where: { id, organization_id } })` (the pattern already used by `credential-vault.repository.ts`), and `update`/`delete`/folder/file operations must verify the parent record's organization before mutating. Alternatively, enforce org checks in the routes and pass `request.user.orgId` into every service call.
evidence: Local unit-level PoC executed against the real route plugins with a faithful in-memory Prisma mock (`tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts`): all 9 assertions passed, including cross-org read (200 + org-B data returned), cross-org file update (`PWNED-BY-ORG-A` written to org-B row), cross-org file delete, and KB rename/soft-delete. vitest output: `Test Files 2 passed, Tests 12 passed`.
assumptions: Any authenticated platform user with a valid membership in any organization (role `member` suffices — `requireModifyAccess` is a role check only).
counterevidence: Checked for mitigations: no `requireScopeAccess`/`requireAgentAccess` on these routes, no org filter in `knowledge-base.service.ts` read/update/delete/findById calls, and no global authz hook in route registration (`src/routes/index.ts` registers `knowledgeBaseRoutes` with a bare prefix). Only `listByOrganization` and `create` scope by org. No WAF or gateway-layer tenant filter exists in this codebase. The local repro follows production Prisma `where`-clause semantics exactly.
severity_change_conditions: If knowledge-base IDs were unguessable and never leaked this would not reduce the demonstrated IDOR; only confirmation of an upstream gateway tenant filter (none exists in this codebase) would lower severity.

title: Cross-tenant IDOR on briefing routes (read/mark-read/archive other organizations' scope briefings)
description: Briefing routes under `/api/business-scopes/:scopeId/briefings` filter only by `business_scope_id` and never by organization or caller membership. Any authenticated user can read another organization's scope briefings (titles, summaries, importance, agent identity) and mark them read or archive them.
impact: Cross-tenant confidentiality and integrity breach on AI-generated business-scope briefings: another tenant's briefing content (titles, summaries, event metadata, agent display names) is disclosed, and read/archive state can be tampered with. Impact limited to briefing objects, hence lower than the KB finding.
technical_analysis: `src/routes/briefing.routes.ts`: all four routes use only `preHandler: [authenticate]`. The GET handler (line ~29) queries `prisma.scope_briefings.findMany({ where: { business_scope_id: scopeId, ... } })` — no organization_id, no scope-membership check. The PATCH/DELETE handlers (lines ~58-84) call `prisma.scope_briefings.update({ where: { id, business_scope_id: scopeId } })` — again no tenant filter; the caller can act on any org's briefing given its scope and briefing IDs. The stats route likewise counts by scope only. Contrast with routes that correctly mount `requireScopeAccess` (e.g. scopeMemberships.routes.ts).
poc_description: 1. Authenticate as member of org A. 2. GET /api/business-scopes/<orgB-scope-id>/briefings — returns org B's briefing list including titles/summaries. 3. PATCH .../briefings/:id/read — flips org B's briefing to read. 4. DELETE .../briefings/:id — archives org B's briefing.
poc_script_code:
# Reproduce (repo-local, no network):
cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts
# C4 assertions:
# - GET    /api/business-scopes/<ORG_B_SCOPE>/briefings          -> 200, contains 'SECRET-BRIEFING'
# - PATCH  /api/business-scopes/<ORG_B_SCOPE>/briefings/<id>/read -> 200, org-B is_read=true
# - DELETE /api/business-scopes/<ORG_B_SCOPE>/briefings/<id>      -> 200, org-B is_archived=true
remediation_steps: Add `organization_id: request.user.orgId` to every `scope_briefings` query, or mount `requireScopeAccess('member')` on these routes so scope membership is verified before the handler runs.
evidence: Local PoC (`tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts`, describe 'C4'): org-A user requests org-B scope briefings — GET returns `SECRET-BRIEFING`; PATCH read flips `is_read` on the org-B row; DELETE sets `is_archived` on the org-B row. All 3 assertions passed (vitest: 12 tests passed).
assumptions: Any authenticated platform user of any organization.
counterevidence: Checked for mitigations: routes carry only `authenticate` (no `requireScopeAccess`, whose default extractor reads `params.scopeId` and would have enforced scope membership). No organization_id filter exists in any briefing query, and the schema has `organization_id` available on `scope_briefings` for enforcement. PoC used faithful Prisma where-clause semantics on real route plugins.
severity_change_conditions: If briefings were confirmed to contain no sensitive content (marketing-only) severity would drop; if they embed document excerpts severity would rise.

title: Path traversal + git argument injection in plugin installation (installPlugins)
description: The scope-plugin installation path (WorkspaceManager.installPlugins) joins an attacker-controlled plugin name into the filesystem without any traversal check, and passes an attacker-controlled git URL into git clone as a positional argument. An authenticated user with modify access on a business scope can make the backend git-clone a repository into an arbitrary directory outside the session workspace (arbitrary file write), and can inject git options such as --upload-pack to execute an arbitrary command.
impact: Arbitrary file/directory write outside the session workspace as the backend process user (locally confirmed: repo cloned into /tmp/marker-plugin via a ../-laden plugin name), and arbitrary command execution via git argv injection (--upload-pack=touch /tmp/marker-uploadpack confirmed). Enables overwriting other tenants' session workspaces (cross-tenant integrity) and planting files into paths later executed or read by the backend/agent runtimes.
technical_analysis: POST /api/business-scopes/:id/plugins (super-agent/backend/src/routes/businessScopes.routes.ts:836) accepts name (only minLength 1 / maxLength 100 — no character or path validation), gitUrl, ref from an authenticated user with modify access, stored raw into scope_plugins. On session provisioning, chat.service.ts buildScopeForWorkspace loads them and WorkspaceManager.ensureSessionWorkspace → installPlugins (src/services/workspace-manager.ts:932) computes `const targetDir = join(pluginsDir, plugin.name)` (line 941) with no containment check, then `execFile('git', ['clone','--depth','1','--branch', plugin.ref, plugin.gitUrl, targetDir])` (lines 949-952). Two primitives: (1) plugin.name containing `../` or an absolute path makes git clone write a full repo tree outside the workspace; (2) plugin.gitUrl is positional but git parses a leading-dash value as an option, so `--upload-pack=<cmd>` or `-o ProxyCommand=…` executes an arbitrary command with backend privileges — execFile's argv-array form does not mitigate option injection. Local replication of the exact sink code confirmed both primitives.
poc_description: 1. POST /api/business-scopes/:id/plugins with name `../../../../../../../tmp/marker-plugin`, gitUrl of any reachable repo, ref main (businessScopes.routes.ts:836; requires only authenticate + requireModifyAccess). 2. Start any chat session in that scope — ensureSessionWorkspace calls installPlugins, which computes targetDir = join(workspace/.claude/plugins, plugin.name) and runs `git clone --depth 1 --branch ref gitUrl targetDir`. 3. Observe the cloned repo written outside the workspace base dir. Command-exec variant: set gitUrl to `--upload-pack=<cmd>`; git parses it as an option and executes it.
remediation_steps: Validate plugin.name and plugin.ref against a strict allowlist (e.g. ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$, no leading dash, no path separators) at the POST /plugins route and again in installPlugins before the join; reject any resolved target whose relative() from pluginsDir escapes it. Reject gitUrl/ref values beginning with a dash and pass them only after a `--` argument separator; allowlist the URL scheme to https/ssh. Apply the same validation to the DELETE plugin cleanup path, which rm -rf's join(sessionsDir, sess.name, '.claude', 'plugins', plugin.name).
evidence: Local harness replicating the exact sink logic: join('/tmp/wsharness/ws/.claude/plugins', '../../../../../tmp/marker-plugin') as clone target → /tmp/marker-plugin/.git created outside workspace (verified via fs.access). Same argv shape with gitUrl='--upload-pack=touch /tmp/marker-uploadpack' → /tmp/marker-uploadpack created, proving option injection into git. Skill-name variant: join(skillsDir, '../../../../../../tmp/marker-evilskill') + mkdir/writeFile produced /tmp/marker-evilskill/SKILL.md; cp(localPath,…) variant produced /tmp/marker-localskill/SKILL.md.
assumptions: Assumes an authenticated org user with modify access on a scope (default member-level permission) and one chat session start to trigger provisioning; no other privileges needed.
counterevidence: Checked all paths for controls: route schema (businessScopes.routes.ts:839) allows any string; DB stores raw; buildScopeForWorkspace passes raw; installPlugins has no name validation. deleteWorkspaceSkill DOES have a startsWith guard (workspace-manager.ts:1420), proving the pattern was known but not applied here. gitUrl must be a clonable URL for the traversal variant, but the --upload-pack variant needs no valid repo.
confidence_rationale: Sink code read in full (complete source→sink trace); escape behavior of join+mkdir/cp and git-clone-into-traversal-path both demonstrated locally with exact code replicated. Only unexecuted step is the full HTTP route round-trip, straight-line code with no intervening sanitization.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the backend runs with privileges that make planted files auto-executed (cron, systemd, module resolution paths) would raise this to critical; a read-only container FS would lower impact but not the vulnerability class.

title: Path traversal via skill/generated-skill names in workspace provisioning (downloadSkill, installSkillToWorkspace, generateAgentSubagentFiles)
description: Skill names flow unvalidated from authenticated-user-controlled and externally-derived sources into path joins in WorkspaceManager.downloadSkill, installSkillToWorkspace, and generateAgentSubagentFiles (generated skills), allowing arbitrary file write outside the workspace root during session workspace provisioning. A skill or generated-skill name containing ../ makes the backend write attacker-controlled SKILL.md content (skill body) to arbitrary paths as the backend process user.
impact: Arbitrary file write (content partially attacker-controlled via skill body / generated-skill body) outside the session workspace, as the backend process user. Enables overwriting config, other tenants' workspaces, or any file writable by the backend user.
technical_analysis: downloadSkill (src/services/workspace-manager.ts:968) computes `const skillDir = join(targetDir, skill.name)` with no traversal check, then either `cp(skill.localPath, skillDir, {recursive:true})` (localPath from skill metadata, also unvalidated) or writes SKILL.md with skill.body/description (inline fallback, lines 1020-1046). skill.name originates from POST /api/skills (skills.routes.ts:51 — no schema on name, only authenticate), marketplace install (name derived from external GitHub/skills.sh content: installRef substring or directory/file names from attacker-hosted repos), zip upload (parent directory name inside an attacker-supplied archive), and generated skills from agent model_config.generatedSkills / tools[].name (agents.routes.ts:177 model_config: additionalProperties true). generateAgentSubagentFiles (workspace-manager.ts:738+) similarly joins skillsDir with generated skill.name and writes SKILL.md, and joins agentsDir with agent.name + '.md'. Session provisioning (ensureSessionWorkspace, called from chat.service on every new chat/session) makes this reachable by any user who can start a chat in a scope with the malicious skill bound. Local replication of the exact join+mkdir+write logic confirmed the out-of-root write.
poc_description: 1. Create a skill via POST /api/skills (skills.routes.ts:51 — no name validation) or via marketplace import whose derived name contains `../` segments, with metadata.body set. 2. Bind the skill to a scope and start a chat session. 3. ensureSessionWorkspace → downloadSkill computes join(skillsDir, skill.name) and writes SKILL.md with the attacker-controlled body — confirmed locally that this lands outside the workspace root.
remediation_steps: Apply a single shared containment helper at the write sites: validate skill/subagent/generated-skill names against ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$ (no separators, no leading dash) at API ingestion (skills.routes.ts create/patch, skill-marketplace install/installFromZip, agents model_config.generatedSkills and tools[].name) and re-check in downloadSkill, installSkillToWorkspace, and generateAgentSubagentFiles that the resolved path stays inside the target directory (reuse the startsWith/relative pattern already present in deleteWorkspaceSkill). Same for agent.name in the .claude/agents/{name}.md join.
evidence: Local harness replicating downloadSkill's exact logic: join(skillsDir, '../../../../../../tmp/marker-evilskill') → mkdir(recursive) + writeFile produced /tmp/marker-evilskill/SKILL.md outside the workspace (verified via fs.access). The cp(localPath, skillDir) variant produced /tmp/marker-localskill/SKILL.md from a local skill source. PoC3 also confirmed zip extraction: python3 -m zipfile -e extracts '../' zip members outside the target directory (marker /tmp/wsharness/extracttest/tmp/marker-zipslip.txt).
assumptions: Authenticated org member (skills POST routes require only `authenticate`). Skill names generated from external GitHub content (skills.sh / probe-github) must be treated as untrusted input.
counterevidence: Searched for sanitization of skill.name at every hop: skills.routes.ts:51 POST /api/skills applies no schema/regex to name; skill.service.createSkill stores raw; buildScopeForWorkspace (chat.service.ts:425-460) maps it raw; downloadSkill and generateAgentSubagentFiles contain no containment checks. The one guard that exists (deleteWorkspaceSkill startsWith, workspace-manager.ts:1420) is not on the write path. installFromZip/GitHub paths derive names from external content rather than validating, which broadens rather than restricts.
confidence_rationale: Sink code read in full and traversal write of SKILL.md confirmed locally; the DB-side control of skill.name (via /api/skills create with unvalidated name) is a direct straight-line path with no intervening sanitization.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating that a planted file is auto-executed by the backend or runtime (module resolution, cron) would raise to critical/high-with-RCE; restricting skill creation to tenant-admin roles would lower privileges_required.

title: Zip-slip in extractSkillZip python3 -m zipfile fallback
description: The skill-archive extraction fallback `python3 -m zipfile -e` does not sanitize archive member paths, so a skill.zip containing `../` members writes files outside the extraction directory (zip-slip) during workspace provisioning.
impact: Arbitrary file write outside the skill directory as the backend process user, when the python3 fallback is used.
technical_analysis: extractSkillZip (src/services/workspace-manager.ts:1049-1061) first tries `unzip -o <zip> -d <dir>` and on failure falls back to `python3 -m zipfile -e <zip> <dir>`. Python's zipfile module extracts member names without path sanitization, so archive members containing `../` escape targetDir. The zip originates from S3 (skill.s3Prefix + 'skill.zip'), i.e. from skill uploads (skill-marketplace installFromZip / upload flows), which accept user-supplied archives. Local PoC confirmed the escape.
poc_description: 1. Upload a skill whose skill.zip contains a member named `../../../../../tmp/marker-zipslip.txt` (stored to S3 via the normal skill upload path). 2. Ensure the extraction path takes the python3 fallback (unzip unavailable/failing on the host). 3. Start a session that provisions the skill — extractSkillZip writes the member outside the skill dir.
poc_script_code:
import zipfile
zipfile.ZipFile('/tmp/wsharness/evil.zip', 'w').write('/etc/hostname', '../../../../../tmp/marker-zipslip.txt')
# then: python3 -m zipfile -e /tmp/wsharness/evil.zip <targetDir>
# locally produced the file outside targetDir (verified).
remediation_steps: Replace the python3 -m zipfile fallback with a sanitizing extractor (reject members with absolute paths or `..` segments, verify resolved destination stays inside targetDir), or drop the fallback and fail closed when unzip is unavailable.
evidence: Local PoC: crafted zip with member `../../../../../tmp/marker-zipslip.txt` extracted with `python3 -m zipfile -e` into a target dir produced the file outside that dir (marker verified on disk).
assumptions: Attacker controls the skill.zip content in S3 (normal skill upload path) and the backend host lacks the `unzip` binary (or unzip fails), triggering the python3 fallback.
counterevidence: Primary path uses system unzip, which refuses `../` members (Info-ZIP behavior) and would block the attack; the python3 fallback only runs when unzip is unavailable or errors. The route only accepts .zip/.tar.gz/.tgz extensions (skill-marketplace.routes.ts:272), which does not constrain archive member names.
confidence_rationale: zip-slip behavior of python3 -m zipfile confirmed locally with a crafted archive; reachability is conditional on the python fallback branch being taken (unzip missing/failing), which is environment-dependent and could not be verified against a deployed host.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the production image lacks `unzip` (forcing the fallback on every extraction) would raise this to high.

title: Hardcoded bypassPermissions with bypassable regex denylist enables unapproved arbitrary shell execution on backend host via agent tool calls
description: The backend's Claude agent runs with a hardcoded `permissionMode: 'bypassPermissions'` and `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true`. The only remaining guard is a small regex denylist (`dangerousCommandBlocker`) that is trivially bypassed, so any prompt the agent acts on — including instructions injected via retrieved documents, skills, or web content — results in arbitrary shell command execution on the backend host without any human approval.
impact: Arbitrary command execution on the backend server (the EC2 host running the Fastify backend, where the Claude CLI subprocess is spawned), outside the intended workspace directory and without any approval step. The executed process inherits the full backend environment, including Bedrock AWS credentials (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`/`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`) and an internal auth token (`AUTH_TOKEN`) explicitly injected into `options.env` — both readable via a single allowed command such as `env`. Host file exfiltration is equally unconstrained (`cat /etc/passwd` variants are only blocked by incidental regex matches, not by policy). Any authenticated user who can chat with an agent — or any attacker who can poison a document, skill, or fetched web page the agent reads — can trigger this.
technical_analysis:
`ClaudeAgentService.buildOptions` constructs the SDK options for every chat conversation:

```ts title=backend/src/services/claude-agent.service.ts startLineNumber=405 endLineNumber=415
const options: ClaudeCodeOptions = {
  systemPrompt,
  allowedTools: [...DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TOOLS, 'Skill'],
  cwd: workspacePath,
  model,
  permissionMode: 'bypassPermissions',
  allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true,
  hooks: { PreToolUse: preToolUseHooks },
```

`DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TOOLS` is `['Bash','Read','Write','Edit','Glob','Grep','WebFetch']` (line 217). With `bypassPermissions`, the Claude Code CLI/SDK executes every tool call without prompting any user. The only security control on this path is the `PreToolUse` hook chain `[dangerousCommandBlocker, binaryFileReadBlocker]` from `claude-hooks.ts`. `dangerousCommandBlocker` compares `tool_input.command` against 7 regexes (5 "dangerous" patterns such as `rm -rf /`, `curl | bash`, plus path-escape patterns matching `..` and absolute paths under a fixed directory list `/Users|home|etc|var|tmp|...`). This is a denylist, not an approval boundary: any command that does not match those literals is executed. Verified locally against the real hook code: `python3 -c "open('/tmp/X','w')"`, `node -e "fs.writeFileSync('/tmp/X')"`, and writes to `$HOME` all pass. The file-path check for Read/Write/Edit uses `filePath.startsWith(cwd)` on the un-normalized string (`claude-hooks.ts:149`), so a path like `<cwd>/../../etc/shadow` passes the containment check. The settings escalation is systemic: `WorkspaceManager` also writes sub-agent definition files containing `permissionMode: bypassPermissions` (`workspace-manager.ts:767`) and a `settings.json` with `permissions.allow` for the same tool list, so the bypass is re-instantiated through the `Skill`/`Task` delegation paths too. Additionally, `buildOptions` copies `...process.env` and Bedrock AWS credentials into the agent subprocess environment (`claude-agent.service.ts:436-449`), so an executed command can read the backend's cloud credentials.
poc_description: 1. Import the repository's real PreToolUse hook `dangerousCommandBlocker` from `backend/src/services/claude-hooks.ts` and instantiate the real `ClaudeAgentService.buildOptions()` with the repo's own `.env`. 2. Confirm the emitted SDK options hardcode `permissionMode: 'bypassPermissions'` and `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true` with `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit`, `WebFetch` in `allowedTools`. 3. Feed the Bash tool input `python3 -c "open('/tmp/PWNED_VIA_HOOK_BYPASS','w')"` through the hook — it returns no block decision (allow). 4. Execute that same command exactly as the SDK's Bash tool would — the marker file `/tmp/PWNED_VIA_HOOK_BYPASS` appears on the host filesystem. 5. Also observe the file_path guard accepts `<cwd>/../../etc/shadow` because it uses an un-normalized `startsWith(cwd)` prefix check.
remediation_steps: Do not hardcode `bypassPermissions` for host-side agent runs. Select a permission mode appropriate to the deployment (e.g. `default` or `acceptEdits`) so that Bash execution and out-of-workspace access require explicit human approval, and make the mode a server-side configuration decision rather than a constant in `buildOptions`. Replace the regex denylist with a positive allowlist enforced at the tool boundary: restrict the Bash tool to an approved command grammar (or run it inside a sandboxed container with no host credentials), canonicalize file paths (`path.resolve`) before the workspace-containment check instead of a raw `startsWith(cwd)` prefix comparison, and do not pass `AWS_*` credentials, `AUTH_TOKEN`, or the rest of `process.env` to the agent subprocess. Network egress from the agent should be restricted so exfiltration via `WebFetch` is not available to injected instructions.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker who can send a chat message to an agent (any authenticated platform user with agent access) or can plant instructions in content the agent reads (skills, RAG results, web pages via WebFetch). Local validation exercised the real guard and execution; live-model end-to-end replay was out of scope (local-only mandate).
counterevidence: Considered defenses: (1) the PreToolUse hook chain is real and registered on every conversation (verified in buildOptions output, PreToolUse hook entries: 1), but it is a fixed 7-regex denylist, not an approval or allowlist — it cannot constrain the input class; (2) cwd confines Write/Edit file_path via startsWith(cwd), but the check is on the un-normalized string and Bash is entirely unconstrained apart from the patterns; (3) no other permission gate exists — permissionMode is hardcoded, not read from request or DB, so no stronger user/org setting can raise it. The only genuine limitation is that this is the intended "dangerous by design" agent mode, which is precisely the control weakness being reported.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that agents are only ever invoked with sanitized/whitelisted prompts and never consume untrusted retrieved content would lower this; conversely, confirming a live deployment reaches the internet with real AWS credentials in the agent environment would cement critical severity.

title: AgentCore runtime executes all agent tool calls with no approval or PreToolUse security hook (bypassPermissions, unfiltered Bash/WebFetch/Write)
description: The AgentCore container runtime (`agentcore/src/agent-runner.ts`) runs the Claude agent with hardcoded `permissionMode: 'bypassPermissions'` and registers **no security hook at all** — its only hooks are S3 file-sync observers. Every tool call, including shell commands, web fetches, and arbitrary file writes, executes with zero approval or filtering, so injected instructions in restored workspace files, RAG results, or fetched web content translate directly into unapproved execution inside the runtime container.
impact: Arbitrary unapproved shell command execution, arbitrary file write, and unrestricted network egress (WebFetch/WebSearch) inside the AgentCore runtime container for any instruction the model acts on — including instructions from prompt-injection sources: workspace files restored from S3 (skills, sub-agent definitions, `CLAUDE.md`), knowledge/RAG results fetched via the injected backend token, and fetched web pages. The container holds the workspace, the `AUTH_TOKEN` backend credential, and any container-resident credentials; the Stop-hook full S3 sync (`syncWorkspaceToS3`) then mirrors attacker-created or modified files back into the organization's persistent S3 workspace, persisting the compromise across sessions.
technical_analysis:
`runAgent()` in `agentcore/src/agent-runner.ts` builds the SDK options for every AgentCore invocation:

```ts title=agentcore/src/agent-runner.ts startLineNumber=283 endLineNumber=289
const baseOptions: Record<string, unknown> = {
  systemPrompt: payload.system_prompt ?? undefined,
  allowedTools: payload.allowed_tools ?? DEFAULT_TOOLS,
  cwd: '/workspace',
  permissionMode: 'bypassPermissions',
  allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true,
```

`DEFAULT_TOOLS` (line 23) includes `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit`, `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`, `Task`, `Skill`. Hooks are registered **only** when S3 workspace sync is configured, and those hooks are `PostToolUse` (matcher `Write|Edit`, uploads the file the tool already wrote) and `Stop` (full workspace upload). A repository-wide search of `agentcore/src/` shows zero `PreToolUse` registrations — unlike the backend runtime (`claude-agent.service.ts`), which at least installs `dangerousCommandBlocker`. So in the AgentCore path there is no security inspection of any tool invocation: the model's tool call goes straight to execution. The prompt itself is attacker-influenceable through several untrusted channels: (a) `restoreWorkspaceFromS3` (`index.ts:46-53`) copies every object under the org/session S3 prefix — including skill `SKILL.md` files, sub-agent `.md` definitions, and `CLAUDE.md` — into `/workspace` before the run, all of which the SDK loads via `settingSources: ['project']`; (b) `index.ts:73-75` sets `process.env.AUTH_TOKEN` from the payload so the agent can query the backend RAG; (c) `WebFetch`/`WebSearch` pull arbitrary web content mid-run. Any instruction embedded in those sources is executed with no approval step, and attacker-written files persist via `syncWorkspaceToS3`.
poc_description: 1. Read `agentcore/src/agent-runner.ts` `runAgent()` and `agentcore/src/index.ts`: confirm `permissionMode: 'bypassPermissions'` + `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true` with `DEFAULT_TOOLS` including `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit`, `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`, `Task`, `Skill`. 2. Enumerate all hook registrations: only `PostToolUse` (S3 sync of Write/Edit results) and `Stop` (full workspace sync) exist — there is no `PreToolUse` security hook in the entire `agentcore/src/` tree. 3. Note the untrusted-content entry points: `restoreWorkspaceFromS3` restores organization-controlled/S3-restored skill and agent files into `/workspace` before the run, and `index.ts` sets `AUTH_TOKEN` from the payload so the agent can call the backend RAG API. Under `bypassPermissions` the SDK executes any Bash tool call derived from these sources immediately — no human approval step exists in this code path. Local-only constraint prevented invoking a live Bedrock AgentCore runtime; the absence of the control is a complete static fact of the executed code path.
remediation_steps: Port the PreToolUse guard chain from the backend runtime into `agent-runner.ts` as a baseline, then move beyond a denylist: default the container runtime to a permission mode requiring approval for Bash and out-of-workspace access (or restrict `allowedTools` per deployment), register a PreToolUse hook that enforces workspace containment via canonicalized path comparison, and restrict outbound network access from the container so injected instructions cannot exfiltrate data or fetch additional payloads via WebFetch/WebSearch. Ensure the injected `AUTH_TOKEN` is scoped to the minimum API surface (read-only RAG search) rather than a full member-role token.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker who can send a chat message to an agent routed to the AgentCore runtime (deployment configured with AGENT_RUNTIME=agentcore), or who can plant instructions in content the agent retrieves (S3-restored skills, RAG results via backend_api_key, WebFetch/WebSearch pages). Consequence boundary (no approval/no PreToolUse filter on Bash/Write/WebSearch) was verified by reading the unmodified runtime code; live end-to-end replay through Bedrock AgentCore was out of scope (local-only mandate, no AWS contact).
counterevidence: Considered: the runtime does register hooks (PostToolUse S3-sync, Stop full sync), but neither intercepts tool execution; `payload.allowed_tools` could theoretically narrow the tool list, but no backend caller sets it (grep shows no producer), so the default full list applies; the container is a microVM, which limits host blast radius relative to the backend-host finding, but the workspace, the injected backend token, and any credentials placed in the container remain fully exposed; `WebFetch`/`WebSearch` have no egress restriction anywhere in the runtime. No control was found that gates or inspects a tool call before execution.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that `payload.allowed_tools` is populated with a restrictive list by the backend in real deployments would lower this; confirmation that microVM isolation plus IAM blocks all credential and S3 reachability would lower confidentiality/integrity impact.

title: Cross-tenant IDOR in userGroups member removal and skill/MCP access-grant endpoints (no org scoping)
description: The user-group member and access-grant endpoints operate on bare group/skill/MCP IDs with no organization scoping. An authenticated user of any tenant can remove members from another tenant's user group and rewrite the full access-grant list (skill and MCP server group access) for another organization's skills and MCP servers.
impact: Cross-tenant integrity: arbitrary removal of members from a foreign tenant's user groups (access revocation/DoS on their workflows), and full rewrite of skill_group_access / mcp_group_access rows for foreign tenants' skills and MCP servers — granting or revoking cross-org access to sensitive skills and MCP tool servers, a lateral-movement primitive.
technical_analysis: Route handlers (`routes/userGroups.routes.ts:147` DELETE /:id/members/:userId, `:160` PUT /skills/:skillId/access, `:182` PUT /mcp/:mcpId/access) pass raw path params straight to the repository. `userGroup.repository.ts` scopes findById/update/delete by organization_id (line 48), but `removeMember` (line 94-98) deletes `user_group_members` by bare `group_id`+`user_id`, `grantSkillAccess` (line 112-120) deletes and re-creates `skill_group_access` by bare `skill_id`, and `grantMcpAccess` (line 144-151) does the same for `mcp_group_access` by bare `mcp_server_id`. `getSkillGroupIds`/`getMcpGroupIds` (lines 122, 153) also leak cross-org group IDs unscoped. No organization_id appears anywhere in these where clauses, so a caller from Org A operating on Org B's IDs succeeds.
poc_description: 1. Authenticate as any user in Org A. 2. DELETE /api/user-groups/:id/members/:userId with a foreign org's group id — userGroupRepository.removeMember deletes by bare group_id+user_id with no org filter. 3. PUT /api/user-groups/skills/:skillId/access (and /mcp/:mcpId/access) with a foreign skill/MCP id — grantSkillAccess/grantMcpAccess first deleteMany by bare skill_id/mcp_server_id then re-create grants, cross-tenant. Local unit PoC (vitest, mocked Prisma) confirms the Prisma where clauses contain no organization scoping.
remediation_steps: Add organization_id to every where clause in userGroup.repository.ts (addMember, removeMember, grantSkillAccess, grantMcpAccess, getSkillGroupIds, getMcpGroupIds) and have route handlers pass request.user.orgId through, matching the pattern already used by findById/update/delete in the same repository.
evidence:
Local vitest harness (mocked Prisma) against the real repositories — 3/3 passed:

```
✓ userGroup.removeMember deletes by bare group_id+user_id
  where = { group_id: 'grp-OTHERORG', user_id: 'victim-user' }   // no organization_id
✓ userGroup.grantSkillAccess rewrites skill access by bare skill_id
  deleteMany where = { skill_id: 'skill-OTHERORG' }               // no organization_id
  createMany data[0] = { skill_id, group_id, granted_by }         // no organization_id
```
assumptions: Authenticated user in any organization; object IDs (groups, skills, MCP servers) obtainable via other list endpoints or leaks.
counterevidence: Checked for controls: requireModifyAccess runs on mutating routes but is a role gate, not an object-ownership check — it never inspects orgId against the target row. Repository has no org filter on removeMember/grantSkillAccess. The same repository's findById/update/delete DO filter by organization_id, confirming org scoping is the intended pattern and is absent only on these sinks.
confidence_rationale: Complete source-to-sink trace with executed local PoC against real route code with mocked Prisma; no live multi-tenant deployment exists to run the HTTP request end-to-end (local-only scope).
severity_change_conditions: A live two-tenant deployment test would confirm end-to-end; if group/skill/MCP IDs proved unguessable in practice, exploitability (attack_complexity) would rise and severity could drop.

title: Cross-tenant IDOR in business-scope membership role update and removal (no org scoping)
description: Business-scope membership update and removal endpoints operate on bare membership IDs with no organization scoping. An authenticated user who is scope-admin of any scope in their own org can change a member's role to 'admin' on, or delete, a scope membership belonging to another organization, escalating or revoking a foreign tenant's members.
impact: Cross-tenant integrity: an org-A scope-admin can grant 'admin' role to any user (including the attacker) on an org-B scope, or remove org-B members from their scopes — privilege escalation into a foreign tenant's agent scopes (which control skills, plugins, IM channels).
technical_analysis: routes/scopeMemberships.routes.ts PATCH /:id/members/:membershipId (line ~115) and DELETE /:id/members/:membershipId (line ~138) call scopeAccessService.updateMemberRole / removeMember with request.params.membershipId only. scopeAccess.service.ts lines 122-128 pass it straight through, and scopeMembership.repository.ts updateRole (line 86-91) and delete (line 96-98) run prisma.scope_memberships.update/delete with where: { id } — no organization_id, and no check that the membership belongs to the scope in the URL path. requireScopeAccess gates on the caller's access to the path scope, not on the target membership's scope or org.
poc_description: 1. Authenticate as a user with admin access to a scope in Org A. 2. PATCH /api/business-scopes/:myScopeId/members/:membershipId with role 'admin', where membershipId belongs to Org B — scopeMembershipRepository.updateRole updates by bare id. 3. DELETE variant removes a foreign membership by bare id. Local unit PoC (vitest, mocked Prisma) confirms the where clause contains only { id } with no organization_id.
remediation_steps: In scopeMembership.repository.ts (updateRole line 86, delete line 96) add organization_id scoping — either filter by the caller's org (passing it from the route handler through scopeAccessService) or first verify the membership's business_scope_id resolves to the caller's organization and to the scope named in the URL path, rejecting mismatches.
assumptions: Authenticated user with viewer access to at least one scope in their own org (to satisfy requireScopeAccess('viewer'/'admin')); membership IDs are returned in scope member listings.
counterevidence: requireScopeAccess('admin') on the mutation routes does verify the caller is an admin of the scope named in the URL path (:id) — but the target row deleted is selected solely by membershipId, which is never checked to belong to that path scope. The enrichment query in the GET members route (profiles.findMany by user_id) is also org-free but only returns public profile fields.
confidence_rationale: Complete source-to-sink trace with executed local PoC against real repository code with mocked Prisma; no live multi-tenant deployment exists to run the HTTP request end-to-end (local-only scope).
severity_change_conditions: A live two-tenant deployment test would confirm end-to-end; if membership IDs proved unguessable in practice, attack_complexity would rise and severity could drop.

title: Cross-tenant IDOR in business-scope plugin/MCP delete and list routes (no org scoping)
description: The business-scope plugin and MCP-server management routes issue DELETE statements scoped only by plugin/assignment ID and scope ID with no organization_id filter, and the plugin/MCP listing routes read cross-org data the same way. An authenticated user of any tenant can delete another tenant's scope plugins (including removing their cloned directories from disk) and detach their MCP server assignments.
impact: Cross-tenant integrity/availability: delete a foreign tenant's scope plugins (also recursively deletes their cloned plugin directories from session workspaces on disk) and detach their MCP server assignments, disrupting foreign tenants' agent capabilities; and read foreign tenants' plugin git URLs and MCP server configs (including host addresses) via the unscoped GET routes.
technical_analysis: In routes/businessScopes.routes.ts the DELETE /:id/plugins/:pluginId handler (lines ~880-927) executes `DELETE FROM scope_plugins WHERE id = ${pluginId}::uuid AND business_scope_id = ${scopeId}::uuid` with no organization_id in the WHERE, then removes cloned plugin directories for that scope. DELETE /:id/mcp-servers/:assignmentId (lines ~1001-1022) executes `DELETE FROM scope_mcp_servers WHERE id = ${assignmentId}::uuid AND business_scope_id = ${scopeId}::uuid` — also unscoped. GET /:id/plugins (~821) and GET /:id/mcp-servers (~940) SELECT by business_scope_id only, leaking foreign plugin git_urls and MCP server configs (host_address, config JSON). The config_version bump after each mutation is scoped by org but only updates the count, not the deletion.
poc_description: 1. Authenticate as any user in Org A. 2. DELETE /api/business-scopes/:scopeId/plugins/:pluginId with Org B's scope ID and plugin ID — the raw SQL deletes by plugin_id + scope_id only; org_id appears in no WHERE clause of the DELETE. 3. The route then removes cloned plugin directories under workspaceBaseDir/<orgB>/<scopeB>/sessions. 4. DELETE /api/business-scopes/:id/mcp-servers/:assignmentId similarly deletes scope_mcp_servers by assignment_id + scope_id only. GET /:id/plugins and /:id/mcp-servers also leak foreign data (plugin git_urls, MCP configs).
remediation_steps: In businessScopes.routes.ts, verify the target scope belongs to the caller's organization (businessScopeService.getBusinessScopeById(id, orgId)) before the DELETE/SELECT statements on plugin delete, plugin list, MCP assignment delete, and MCP list — matching the verification already present on the POST routes.
evidence:
Route code (businessScopes.routes.ts):

```sql
-- DELETE /:id/plugins/:pluginId (line ~894)
DELETE FROM scope_plugins WHERE id = ${pluginId}::uuid AND business_scope_id = ${scopeId}::uuid
-- DELETE /:id/mcp-servers/:assignmentId (line ~1011)
DELETE FROM scope_mcp_servers WHERE id = ${assignmentId}::uuid AND business_scope_id = ${scopeId}::uuid
-- GET /:id/plugins (line ~821) and GET /:id/mcp-servers (line ~940): SELECT ... WHERE business_scope_id = ${id}::uuid
```
assumptions: Authenticated user; business-scope IDs obtainable via listings or shared with the same attacker via showcase packs.
counterevidence: POST plugin and POST mcp-servers routes DO verify scope ownership via businessScopeService.getBusinessScopeById(id, orgId) before writing — confirming the codebase's intended pattern, absent only on the delete/list routes. requireModifyAccess is a role gate, not an ownership check. Note org_id only appears in the config_version bump UPDATE, which does not restrict the DELETE statements.
confidence_rationale: Complete source-to-sink trace verified directly in route code (raw SQL where clauses read verbatim); no live deployment available for HTTP-level reproduction (local-only scope).
severity_change_conditions: A live two-tenant deployment test would confirm end-to-end; if the raw DELETE affected 0 rows for foreign scopes due to an unverified DB-level control, severity would drop.
